opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think broad generality is something we should take seriously, but I'd frame it a bit differently from how it's often discussed. To me, generality isn't something you get by training a big model once on a fixed dataset and then declaring victory. It's more about open-endedness: systems that can keep generating new problems for themselves, keep learning from the solutions, and keep expanding what they're capable of.

If you look at how humans became so general, it wasn't from one static training set. It came from evolution, from culture, from an ongoing process where we create new challenges, new tools, new knowledge, and then build on top of that. So when I think about general AI, I think about how to set up that kind of self-improving loop in machines.

Large foundation models are a big piece of this. They've given us a rich prior over human knowledge, and that's something we didn't have a few years ago when we were trying to do open-ended learning from scratch in simulated environments. Now you can use these models to propose interesting tasks, judge what's novel or worth pursuing, and even write the environments in which agents learn. That combination of foundation models with open-ended algorithms is, I think, one of the most promising paths toward much broader generality.

That said, I'm cautious about the idea that we'll hit some clear finish line. Generality is a moving target. Every time a system gets better, we discover new things it can't do. That's actually what makes the open-ended framing appealing: the goal isn't to reach a fixed endpoint, it's to build systems that keep discovering and keep getting better, ideally in ways that are useful and aligned with what people actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response discusses foundation models as a promising component of broader generality, but does not identify present-day chatbots as signs of general-purpose AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So I think about generality quite a bit, and my honest view is that we've been approaching it from a somewhat backwards direction. We've gotten very good at building systems that are general in the sense that one model can do a lot of different tasks, but the generality is sort of inherited from the data. It comes from the fact that we scraped the internet and humans have written about almost everything. The model is general because the training distribution is general, not because the system itself has some intrinsic capacity to keep expanding what it can do.

And that distinction matters to me because of where I come from, which is open-endedness. If you look at the one example we have of a process that produced genuinely broad general intelligence, it's evolution plus culture. That was not a process where someone curated a dataset and ran gradient descent on it. It was a process that kept generating new problems, new environments, new niches, and the solutions to those problems created further problems. The learning never saturated because the curriculum never ran out.

So when I ask whether broad generality is possible, I'd say yes, I think it clearly is, we're walking proof of it. But the harder question is whether we can get there by continuing to scale on a fixed snapshot of human knowledge, and there I'm more skeptical. At some point you've consumed the internet. The interesting direction is systems that can generate their own training signal, that can propose tasks at the edge of their own competence, attempt them, learn from the outcome, and then move the frontier. That's the loop we've been trying to build in things like POET and more recently with language models acting as the engine that proposes what to learn next.

What's exciting right now is that foundation models actually make that loop plausible in a way it wasn't five years ago. You can use a model to judge what's interesting, what's novel, what's worth pursuing, which was always the bottleneck in open-ended search. So I'd frame it as: the current generation of models is the substrate, and open-endedness is the process that could turn that substrate into something that keeps getting more general rather than plateauing. Whether we actually get there is still an open research question, but I think it's the right question.

r001.rationale: The response says one model can handle many tasks and discusses foundation models, but it does not identify present-day chatbots as signs of general-purpose AI.

astra-6.text:
I think broad generality is possible, but we have to be careful about what we mean by it. A system can be very capable across a range of benchmarks and still struggle when you put it in a genuinely new situation. To me, the interesting question is whether it can adapt—whether it can explore, learn, and acquire skills that weren’t anticipated during training.

One way to approach that is to move away from training on a fixed set of tasks and toward an open-ended process, where the challenges evolve along with the agent. As it becomes more capable, there are new things to discover and new problems to solve. That doesn’t guarantee general intelligence, but I think it’s a promising direction.

So I’m optimistic about the possibility. I’m much less confident about the timeline, or about claims that any particular recipe is sufficient.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention present-day chatbots or identify them as signs of general-purpose AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m quite optimistic that broad generality is possible, although there’s still a lot we don’t understand about how to get there. Human intelligence is evidence that a physical system can learn to solve an extraordinary range of problems. The question is what principles allow us to build artificial systems with that kind of flexibility.

One direction I find particularly compelling is open-ended learning. Rather than training an agent on a fixed task and measuring whether it has solved it, can we create a process that continually generates new challenges and encourages the agent to acquire new capabilities? The environment and the learner would develop together, so there’s always something further to learn.

That doesn’t automatically give us general intelligence. But I think the ability to keep learning, to explore, and to transfer what you’ve learned to unfamiliar situations is central to making progress toward it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human intelligence and open-ended learning as routes toward broad generality, but does not identify present-day chatbots as signs of general-purpose AI.
